title: The Opposites of Virtues
english: On the vices opposed to the virtues (under the name of Nilus of Ancyra). By the same author, a discourse to the same addressee, on the vices that are the counterparts of the virtues. Chapter 1. I consider it necessary also to set down in summary the vices that are the counterparts of the virtues, for your love of labor; seeing that thus far, having plowed the mind, we have cast the thorns of the thoughts out of the sown land. We have not attained to this by works which we ourselves have done, but having a pattern of sound words which we heard from the Fathers, and having become witnesses of some of the deeds.

But the whole is grace from above, which also shows to sinners the plots of the mind-deceivers, and which secures us, saying: ‘For what do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Cor 4:7), so that through receiving we may give thanks to the Giver, since we do not attribute to ourselves any boast of glory, denying the gift. Therefore he says, ‘But if you did receive, why do you boast as if you had not received?’ (1 Cor 4:7) — ‘Already,’ he says, ‘you have become rich’ — you who toil in works; already you who have begun to be taught have been satiated — whose error has just now passed over into me; through which I have borrowed reasoning, concealing the poverty of my works, and through which I gave counsel with judgment, perverting the discipleship of being taught.

But nevertheless, if any forgiveness is held in store by you, grant it to me as well, so that we too may set down in summary, indicating, the vices that are the counterparts of the virtues: what gluttony is, against which is self-control; what fornication is, and temperance; what love of money is, and non-possession; sorrow, against which is joy; what anger is, and long-suffering; and listlessness, and endurance; what vainglory is, and freedom from vainglory; envy, and freedom from envy; pride, and humility.
